question:
Patient note:
An 83-year-old male was brought to the outpatient medicine clinic by his daughter because of gradually worsening pain in the right calf with walking two short city blocks and a non-healing shallow ulcer over the dorsum of the same foot that has been present for about three weeks. He reports that the discomfort is cramp-like, begins reliably after ambulating a similar distance, and is relieved with rest; he does not feel chest tightness, dyspnea, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea during or after these episodes. He has lived independently in a single-story home, manages his own finances, cooks simple meals, and remains fully oriented to date, place, and situation without any memory lapses noted by family or the primary caregiver. His past medical history is notable for an ischemic stroke affecting the left hemisphere six years ago, from which he recovered fully without residual weakness or speech difficulty; he completed a course of dual antiplatelet therapy at that time and has remained on low-dose aspirin alone since. He also carries a long-standing diagnosis of type 2 diabetes that was discovered twenty years earlier during an employment physical; the condition has been controlled with metformin 1 g twice daily, and his most recent primary-care record, dated six months ago, documented an HbA1c of 6.8 %, normal monofilament sensation in both feet, and no evidence of retinopathy on annual ophthalmologic screening. Two years ago, a surveillance abdominal ultrasound done for mildly elevated aminotransferases demonstrated a coarsened hepatic echotexture without nodularity, and subsequent laboratory work revealed a normal synthetic profile (albumin 4.2 g/dL, INR 1.1, platelet count 200 000/µL) and no bilirubin elevation, leading his gastroenterologist to attribute the findings to non-alcoholic fatty infiltration; he has never developed ascites, variceal bleeding, or hepatic encephalopathy. He denies any prior myocardial infarction, valve surgery, cardiac stents, or episodes of decompensated heart muscle weakness. He has never experienced transient focal neurological deficits suggestive of a transient ischemic attack. He also denies chronic lung conditions such as COPD or asthma, has no history of peptic or duodenal ulcer disease or gastrointestinal bleeding, and has not been diagnosed with any solid-organ or hematologic malignancy, including lymphoma. He has never tested positive for HIV and has no history of AIDS or other immunodeficiency. His only surgical procedure has been an endovascular balloon angioplasty of the right superficial femoral artery performed eight years ago for similar calf claudication, after which his symptoms improved for several years. He stopped smoking 35 pack-years ago, drinks red wine on special occasions only, and has never used illicit drugs. Family history is significant for hypertension and diabetes in first-degree relatives but no premature coronary disease or malignancy. He is allergic to penicillin (rash). Medications include metformin as noted, low-dose aspirin, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and vitamin D. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, weight loss, hemoptysis, chronic cough, wheezing, ankle swelling, transient vision loss, double vision, or seizures. On examination, he is a thin older gentleman appearing stated age, blood pressure 124/64 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.8 °C, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Mental status is intact with fluent speech, appropriate naming, and normal short- and long-term recall. Cardiovascular exam reveals a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Lungs are clear bilaterally to auscultation and percussion. Abdomen is soft, nontender, with no hepatosplenomegaly and no fluid wave. Peripheral vascular assessment shows normal brachial and radial pulses symmetrically, diminished right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses compared with the left, and an ankle-brachial index measured by Doppler of 0.52 on the right and 0.78 on the left. The right foot ulcer is 1.2 cm in diameter with a pale base and minimal serous drainage, surrounded by hairless, cool skin; there is no surrounding cellulitis. Sensory examination with a 10-g monofilament is intact at all plantar surfaces, and motor strength is full in all extremities. Laboratory data obtained this morning show hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 78 mL/min/1.73 m²), fasting glucose 132 mg/dL, AST 54 U/L, ALT 62 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 112 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, INR 1.0, LDL 82 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 3 mg/L. Urinalysis is unremarkable with no proteinuria or hematuria. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without Q-waves or ST-T abnormalities. A duplex ultrasound of the right lower extremity ordered today demonstrates significant atherosclerotic plaque with 70 % stenosis in the superficial femoral artery and monophasic flow in the distal popliteal segment; no acute thrombosis is visualized. Given the progressive exertional calf pain, diminished distal pulses, and non-healing ulcer, the working diagnosis is lower-extremity ischemia on the background of established systemic atherosclerosis. The patient will be scheduled for vascular surgery consultation and noninvasive imaging to delineate the arterial tree further, while attention to glycemic control, lipid lowering, antiplatelet therapy, and walking exercise will continue.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index adds age points to weighted points for qualifying chronic conditions.
- Age 83 (≥80 years): 4.
- Peripheral vascular disease: claudication, prior femoral angioplasty, and right ABI 0.52 establish symptomatic arterial disease: 1.
- Cerebrovascular disease: prior ischemic stroke without residual hemiplegia: 1.
- Diabetes without documented diabetic end-organ damage: metformin-treated type 2 diabetes; the foot ulcer is attributed to arterial ischemia: 1.
- Mild liver disease: chronic fatty liver disease with preserved synthetic function and no evidence of portal hypertension: 1.
No other qualifying comorbidity is documented. Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8.
Final answer: 8
